definition: First troubleshooting step: gather information, question users, identify symptoms, find out what has changed, and duplicate the issue if possible.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

term: Establish a theory of probable cause
definition: Second troubleshooting step: make an educated guess about the source of the issue, starting with simple causes and using approaches such as working through the OSI layers.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Third troubleshooting step: confirm the suspected cause; if it is confirmed, decide the next steps, and if not, form a new guess or escalate.
acceptedAnswers: Test the theory to determine the cause
Test the theory to determine cause
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Fourth troubleshooting step: decide how to fix the confirmed cause, when to make the change, who is involved, and what side effects it may have on users.
acceptedAnswers: Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and identify potential effects
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Fifth troubleshooting step: apply the planned fix one change at a time, after warning affected users and saving current settings, or pass the issue to higher support.
acceptedAnswers: Implement the solution or escalate as necessary
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking

definition: Sixth troubleshooting step: confirm that the whole system works after the fix, ideally with the user, and add preventive measures so the issue does not return.
acceptedAnswers: Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures if applicable
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Seventh and final troubleshooting step: record the symptoms, cause, fix, results, who did the work, and lessons learned, often in a ticket system or knowledge base.
acceptedAnswers: Document findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned
Document findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned throughout the process
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Habit of checking the simplest causes first, such as power, a loose cable, or a disabled port, before suspecting a complex fault.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Troubleshooting approach that starts at the application layer and works down the layers, suited to faults that look software related, such as a rejected password.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking

definition: Troubleshooting approach that starts at the physical layer, ruling out cables and NICs first, and then works up the layers toward the application.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking

definition: Troubleshooting approach that splits a problem into parts, such as separate symptoms or network segments, and rules out each working part until the fault is isolated.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking

definition: Handing an issue to a higher support tier, a specialist, or a supervisor when fixing it is beyond your knowledge, access, or authority.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Information-gathering task of making the fault happen again on purpose, which confirms the symptoms and later proves that the real cause was found.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Way to handle a user who reports several faults at once: rank them by business importance and solve each one separately so causes and fixes stay clear.
acceptedAnswers: Approach multiple problems one at a time
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Information-gathering question that looks for recent patches, new software or hardware, a moved computer, or new credentials, since most faults follow some change.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Noise created when the signal on one wire pair or cable bleeds into an adjacent pair or cable; more twists per foot and shielding reduce it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Signal bleed between wire pairs measured at the same end as the transmitter, often caused by pairs untwisted too far at a poorly made connector.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Signal bleed between wire pairs measured at the opposite end of the cable from the transmitter, after the signal has traveled the full length.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Signal bleed between two separate cables that are bundled or run close together, rather than between the wire pairs inside one cable.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Noise from motors, power lines, fluorescent lights, and other electrical equipment that corrupts signals on copper cable; rerouting, shielded cable, or fiber avoids it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Loss of signal power as a signal travels away from its source, measured in decibels; it limits runs to a set length, such as 100 meters for twisted pair.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Fault in which the cable does not suit the link, such as multimode on a single-mode port, Cat 5 on a 10 Gbps run, or UTP where STP is needed.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Badly attached connector, such as wire pairs untwisted too far or wires not fully seated, that causes signal loss, near-end crosstalk, reflections, and errors.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Fault in which the sending and listening wire pairs or fiber strands are connected the wrong way round, so one device's output never reaches the other's input.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Cable fault in which one or more wires are broken or cut, so the circuit is not complete and a cable tester shows no continuity on them.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Cable fault in which bare wires touch, so current flows onto a wire it was not meant for, often from damaged insulation or a crushed cable.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Dust, oil, or liquid on a fiber end face that blocks light, causing signal loss and errors; inspect it and clean it, with isopropyl alcohol if needed.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Running totals a switch or router keeps for each port, such as errors, runts, giants, and discards, shown by show interface; values that keep rising point to a fault.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Counter entry for a frame whose checksum, recalculated by the receiver, does not match the value sent, usually caused by interference, a damaged cable, or a faulty NIC.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Ethernet frame smaller than the 64-byte minimum, usually the result of a collision or a transmission error; the receiving interface discards it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Ethernet frame larger than the maximum allowed size, often caused by an MTU mismatch or a faulty NIC; the receiving interface discards it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Frames or packets that a device discards instead of delivering, often because of full buffers, congestion, or faults, which leads to lost data and retransmissions.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Port status in which the switch shuts an interface down by itself after it detects a problem, such as a loopback, a duplex mismatch, or a port security violation.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Port status that means a network administrator turned the interface off on purpose, for example with the shutdown command, so it passes no traffic until re-enabled.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Port status for a link aggregation member whose settings, such as speed or VLANs, do not match the other members, so the switch keeps it out of the bundle.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: PoE fault in which the connected devices draw more total wattage than the switch or injector can supply, so it cuts power to some ports.
acceptedAnswers: Power over Ethernet power budget exceeded
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: PoE fault in which a device needs more wattage than the port's version supplies, for example a PoE+ (802.3at) camera on an 802.3af port, so it fails to power up.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Fault in which the optical modules at the two ends of a link differ in standard, speed, or wavelength, such as short-range against long-range, so the link fails or errs.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Fault in which fiber cables with different cores are joined, such as single-mode to multimode or 50-micron to 62.5-micron, so much of the light is lost.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Calculation of how much light power a fiber connection can lose to distance, splices, and connectors while still delivering a usable signal; a low value causes errors and downtime.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Weakening of a light signal as it travels along a fiber and through splices and connectors, measured in decibels with an optical power meter.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Received light level that a fiber transceiver reports, usually in dBm; a level below or above the module's rated range causes errors or a down link.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Redundant path between switches that lets frames circle endlessly, because Ethernet frames carry no time-to-live value; Spanning Tree Protocol prevents it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Flood of broadcast frames, often caused by a switching loop, that uses up bandwidth and switch resources until the network slows or stops.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Single switch that STP elects, by the lowest bridge ID (priority plus MAC address), as the reference point for calculating every loop-free path.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port role on a non-root switch: the one port with the lowest-cost path to the root bridge, which forwards traffic toward it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port role chosen on each network segment as the forwarding port with the lowest cost to the root bridge; every port on the root bridge has this role.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port role for a backup path to the root bridge that stays blocked to prevent a loop but can take over if the root port fails.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Most efficient route from a switch to the root bridge, based on the total of the link costs, which STP uses to choose root ports.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port state that receives BPDUs but forwards no user frames; redundant ports stay in it to prevent loops, and new ports wait in it for 20 seconds.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port state lasting about 15 seconds in which the port sends and receives BPDUs to work out the topology but forwards no frames and adds no MAC addresses.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port state lasting about 15 seconds in which the port adds source MAC addresses to its table but does not yet forward user frames.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Only STP port state that passes user frames to their destinations, while the port keeps reading BPDUs and adding MAC addresses to its table.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: STP port state of a port that is shut down, so it takes no part in spanning tree calculations and passes no user traffic.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: List a router keeps of known destination networks, each with a next hop or exit interface, a metric, and a source such as connected, static, or a routing protocol.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Catch-all 0.0.0.0/0 entry in the table that a router uses when no more specific entry matches a destination; without it, packets to unknown networks are discarded.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Next-hop router that a 0.0.0.0/0 entry points to, which receives every packet the local router cannot match to a known network.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Routing fault in which no entry exists for a destination network and no catch-all entry is configured, so the router discards that traffic as unreachable.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: DHCP fault in which every address in the scope is leased, so new clients get none and fall back to 169.254.x.x addresses; enlarge the scope or shorten the lease time.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Misconfiguration in which a host points to the wrong router address, so it can reach devices on its own subnet but nothing on other networks or the internet.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Conflict in which two devices on one network use the same address, often a static setting that overlaps a DHCP lease, causing warnings and unreliable connections.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Host configured with an address outside its subnet or with a typing error, so it cannot talk to the local network even though the cable and link are fine.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Misconfiguration in which a host's mask does not match its network, so it misjudges which addresses are local and has failed or very limited connectivity.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Switch port placed in the wrong virtual LAN, so the attached device joins another segment and cannot reach the resources it needs.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Rule set on a router, switch, or firewall that permits or denies the wrong traffic, either blocking needed services or, more often, allowing too much.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Condition in which more traffic tries to cross a link or device than it can carry, causing queuing delays, dropped packets, and lower throughput.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Competition among many devices or users for the same shared medium or resource at the same time, which cuts each one's share and causes collisions or waiting.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Single component, such as a slow link or an underpowered router, whose limited capacity caps the performance of the whole data path.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Theoretical maximum amount of data a link or medium can carry in a given time, such as 1 Gbps on a copper Ethernet link.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Actual amount of data delivered per second on a link in real conditions, usually lower than the rated maximum because of overhead, errors, and competing traffic.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Time delay for data to travel from source to destination, measured in milliseconds; high values make voice, video, and interactive applications feel slow.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Failure of some packets to arrive at all, caused by congestion, full buffers, faulty cables, or interference, which forces TCP resends and leaves gaps in real-time audio.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Variation in the delay between arriving packets, measured in milliseconds, which makes voice and video calls choppy even when every packet arrives.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Radio noise from other transmitters on the same frequencies, such as microwave ovens, cordless phones, Bluetooth, or nearby networks, that disrupts a WLAN signal.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Problem where nearby access points use 2.4 GHz channels whose frequency ranges partly share spectrum; avoided by using only channels 1, 6, and 11.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Slowdown when nearby access points use exactly the same channel, so all their clients must take turns on the air and wait for each other.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Weakening of a wireless signal between access point and client because of distance, walls, absorption, or low transmit power, which lowers RSSI and data rates.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Dead or weak areas where no access point gives a usable signal, found with a site survey heat map and fixed by adding or moving APs.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Problem where a wireless device keeps dropping its connection to the access point, often from a weak signal, a crowded channel, or a deauthentication attack.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Setup error, such as access points with different SSIDs or security settings, that stops clients from moving smoothly from one AP to the next.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Signal-strength setting that decides when a wireless client leaves its current access point for a stronger one; a poor value makes clients cling or hop too often.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Condition where more devices join one access point than it can serve, so each device gets less airtime and the whole WLAN slows down.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Utility that sends ICMP echo requests to a host and reports each reply and its round-trip time; the first test of basic reachability.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Linux, UNIX, and macOS utility that lists each router hop to a destination, by default sending UDP probes with rising TTL values.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: Windows utility that lists each router hop to a destination by sending ICMP echo requests with increasing TTL values.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: Reachability test that uses address-resolution requests instead of ICMP, so it works when ICMP is blocked but only within the local subnet.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Windows and Linux utility, with an interactive mode, that queries DNS servers to resolve a name or address and check specific record types.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Linux and macOS DNS query utility with no interactive mode that shows detailed answer and authority sections plus the query time.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Windows command that shows each adapter's IP address, mask, and gateway; /all adds DNS and DHCP lease details, and /release and /renew refresh a lease.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Older Linux, UNIX, and macOS command for viewing and setting network interface addresses, now largely replaced on Linux by a newer utility.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Current Linux command, with subcommands such as addr, route, and link, that shows and changes interface addresses, routes, and link state.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Command that shows or edits the local cache that maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses; -a lists entries and -s adds a static one.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Command that lists the host's active TCP and UDP connections and listening ports; -a shows all, -r the routing table, and -s per-protocol statistics.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Free Linux and UNIX command-line tool that captures packets from a network interface and prints them or saves them to a file for analysis.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: Windows and Linux command that displays or edits the host's own routing table; on Windows, the print option lists it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Simple command that prints the name of the computer it is run on, useful to confirm which host a session is on.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Hardware or software tool that captures traffic and decodes each protocol's headers into readable form, used to find protocol errors, unwanted traffic, and per-protocol bandwidth use.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Free open-source scanner for Windows and Linux that probes a host or address range to report open ports, running services, and operating system details.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Vendor-neutral IEEE 802.1AB Layer 2 protocol that lets switches, routers, and phones from any maker advertise their identity and capabilities to directly connected neighbors.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Proprietary Layer 2 neighbor protocol that shares device type, model, software version, IP address, and port, and works only between one vendor's devices.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Website or app that measures a connection's actual upload and download rates, used to check whether an ISP delivers the promised service.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Public server, often run by an ISP, that offers read-only ping, trace, and BGP route information from its own location on the Internet backbone.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Program that provides a text command-line window, used to run local utilities or reach a remote device's console through SSH.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Two-part kit in which one unit puts an audible signal on a wire pair and a handheld wand detects it, used to trace and identify a cable run.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Handheld device that checks a copper or fiber run for continuity, opens, shorts, and miswired or crossed pairs, giving a pass or fail result.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Passive in-line device placed between two network devices that copies all traffic on that link to a monitoring tool without affecting the flow.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Software that lists nearby wireless networks with their channels and signal strengths, used to choose a clear channel and a good access point location.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Pen-sized tool that shines a visible red laser into a fiber strand so breaks, tight bends, and bad connectors glow, and confirms end-to-end continuity.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 10: Network Troubleshooting

definition: Device that scans a band of radio frequencies for all signals and noise, including non-802.11 sources such as microwaves, to find where interference is greatest.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Switch command that lists which MAC addresses the switch has learned on each port and in each VLAN.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Router command that displays the routing table, with codes for connected, static, and dynamically learned routes and the gateway of last resort.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Device command that displays each port's up or down link state, speed, duplex, MTU, and counters for errors and dropped packets.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Device command that displays the active configuration held in RAM, which is lost at reboot unless copied to the startup file.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Router or switch command that lists the device's table of IP addresses mapped to MAC addresses for hosts it talks to directly.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Switch command that lists each configured VLAN with its number, name, status, and the access ports assigned to it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Switch command that reports the status of installed power supplies and, with the inline option, the PoE power each port draws.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: Router command that prints a short one-line summary for each port with its Layer 3 address and up or down status.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking
